name: al-Baladhuri
label: Outside witness
otherNames: Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Jabir al-Baladhuri (Philip Hitti)
knownFor: A Muslim historian of Baghdad whose Futuh al-Buldan tells how the Muslim conquests were won. It records the terms made with Christian peoples and the fate of churches such as Saint John's at Damascus.
dates: Died in 892, the year 279 of the hijra, by Philip Hitti from the older Arab lives. No source used here gives his birth

keyWorks.title: Futuh al-Buldan
keyWorks.about: the conquests, land by land, with the terms made with each people. Hitti says it is a digest of a larger work that is lost. Held in Hitti's English, volume 1

keyWorks.title: Ansab al-Ashraf (Lineage of Nobles)
keyWorks.about: of which Hitti says two volumes survive. Not held

traces: His book keeps the terms made with Christian peoples, among them Najran, Damascus and the Nubians.
Hitti says the geographer Yakut reproduces a great part of the book, and that later historians drew freely on it.
remembered: Al-Mas'udi, as Hitti quotes him: "We know of no better work on the history of the Moslem conquests".
Richard Gottheil, in his foreword to Hitti, calls the book one of the chief authorities for the forming of the Arab state.

uncertain: He writes as a Muslim historian of the conquests, from reports passed down to him. His life is known from later Arab lives, as Hitti gives them.
How far to trust him. Hitti finds the book free from exaggeration and sincere in seeking the fact. He also says the author scarcely judges what he reports.
The shortened book. Hitti and Gottheil say the Futuh is a digest of a larger work, now lost. Hitti says some passages are mutilated and ambiguous.
His sources. Hitti says he mostly follows the tradition of Medina, and that many of his authorities' works are lost.
How he died. Hitti reports from the older lives that he lost his mind from drinking anacardia juice. That story also explains his name.
